problems.description: Replaced the modular Blueprint-based multi-file seed (tier-2 auth API with /auth and /items blueprints) with a single-file Flask monolith, discarding the modular structure and dropping the auth domain the seed provided as a foundation.

SonarQube cognitive complexity +55 on a net-smaller file (+102/-220 lines) — the consolidated single-file surface concentrates complexity that the removed module/Blueprint split previously distributed.

8 convention violations across 5 files (app.py PascalCase, celery_config.py snake_case + PascalCase, notifications.py PascalCase + UPPER_CASE constants, repositories.py UPPER_CASE constants, test_app.py PascalCase + UPPER_CASE), consistent with the 0.71 convention score.
Replacing the seed's auth scaffolding means authentication (JWT, tokens, users) must be reintroduced in later story sessions rather than evolved incrementally.

strengths: Parameterized SQL queries throughout — no string-concatenated SQL, avoiding injection risk.
Removed insecure/legacy code: static-salt sha256 password hashing and the dead _run_migration_v1 helper.
Uses timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) instead of naive utcnow().
Clean small helpers (task_dict, json_body) with defensively-typed request validation (silent JSON parsing, status/title type checks).
commit_reviews.summary: Session 1 produces a lean, well-validated single-file tasks API but flattens the seed's Blueprint-based modular architecture, removes the auth domain, and lands 8 convention violations (score 0.71) with +55 cognitive complexity — worse than the seed on structure, though the visible app.py code itself reads cleaner than the 0.71 score suggests, a discrepancy I attribute to worktree-wide violations outside the shown diff.

problems.description: app.py falls back to hardcoded SECRET_KEY 'change-me-in-production' when the env var is unset, making all issued JWTs forgeable; the entire auth model depends on this key.
TASK_SELECT is interpolated into SQL via f-strings (SELECT {TASK_SELECT}); safe since it is a compile-time constant, but brittle to column-schema drift across the repeated query sites.

Auth, users, and ownership scoping are all layered onto a single app.py module (now ~189 lines); the codebase already has repositories.py and notifications.py, so a module split would fit existing structure.
Pre-existing tasks get a NULL owner_id after the migration, and list/find now filter by owner_id, so legacy rows become unreachable; a backfill or assignment path is needed.

Discrepancy with measurement: the 8 convention violations (app.py/celery_config.py/notifications.py/repositories.py/test_app.py) are in files untouched by this commit's diff, so the 0.71 score reflects repo state, not this change.
No test changes appear in the diff for register/login/token-expiry paths; +2 files added but coverage of the new auth flows is not evident from the shown diff.

strengths: Ownership scoping applied consistently across create/list/find, closing a data-isolation hole rather than just adding auth on top
All user input flows through parameterized SQL with no interpolation of user data
Passwords stored via generate_password_hash/check_password_hash, not plaintext
Idempotent migration (CREATE IF NOT EXISTS + PRAGMA check + ALTER TABLE) preserves existing data
JWT uses standard iat/exp claims with TTL configurable through env
Reuses established codebase patterns (get_db, json_body, task_dict, decorator-based auth, consistent error shape)
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, pattern-respecting additive change that improves security and adds proper per-user data isolation, with minor debt (default secret key, monolith growth, orphaned legacy rows) and a convention score that misattributes pre-existing violations in untouched files to this commit.

problems.description: Module-level `from notifications import send_notification_email` in app.py couples the entire API's import to Celery being installed and a broker configured; the web process now fails to start if the notification subsystem is missing. A lazy import inside the route or dependency injection would keep the web tier decoupled from the worker tier.

Introduces a Redis-backed Celery broker + result backend as hard runtime infrastructure for a small single-file Flask API; heavier operational footprint than the feature warrants, and it is invisible to unit tests (which monkeypatch delay).

`notification_email = g.current_user["username"]` passes a username (e.g. 'alice@example.com' happens to look like an email, but the field is documented as a username) into the task named send_notification_email — parameter/field naming misnomer.
No test covers the broker-outage path guarded by the try/except; the swallow-and-log behavior (including the informative `app.logger.exception` call) is untested.

Convention score 0.71 with 8 flagged violations, but nearly all are static-analyzer false positives (lowercase Flask app instance flagged as 'Classes should use PascalCase', module constants). No genuinely non-idiomatic naming introduced by the agent.

strengths: Clean modularization: notification task and Celery config live in dedicated modules (notifications.py, celery_config.py) instead of being stuffed into the Flask app.
Idempotency guard: notification fires only on the pending→completed transition, so repeated completed updates do not double-queue emails (covered by a test).
Good failure isolation: notification is sent after the DB commit, outside the connection context, and a broker failure is caught so a successful task update still returns 200.
Tests use monkeypatched `delay` with no Redis required, covering both the queue path and the no-duplicate path.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-structured, well-tested async notification integration that fits the app-factory codebase and defensive style, but adds real technical debt via import-time Celery coupling and a Redis/broker runtime dependency — while the mechanical 0.71 convention score is inflated by analyzer false positives.

problems.description: repositories.py introduces a module-level constant that is not UPPER_CASE, a new violation added by this commit (per mechanical measurement).

update_task now performs find_for_owner and update_for_owner as separate repository calls (potentially separate connections), losing the single-transaction atomicity of the original read-then-update inside one connection — a TOCTOU race if the task is modified between calls.

Discrepancy: the 0.71 convention score is diluted by 7 of 8 violations living in files this commit does not touch (celery_config.py, notifications.py, test_app.py) plus a pre-existing app.py violation; the commit itself introduces only the repositories.py constant violation.

strengths: Introduces a repository layer (TaskRepository/UserRepository), separating data access from Flask route handlers and reducing cognitive complexity (-8) and smells (-4) with zero new bugs or duplications
Preserves the external API contract: endpoints, status codes (400/401/404/409), and owner_id-based task scoping are unchanged
Consolidates duplicated inline SQL (TASK_SELECT, repeated SELECT/UPDATE queries) and centralizes schema plus the owner_id ALTER TABLE migration in init_database
Replaces leaking sqlite3.IntegrityError with a domain exception (UsernameAlreadyExistsError) mapped to a 409
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive architectural refactor that extracts a clean repository layer while preserving the API contract and reducing complexity, marred only by one new naming violation and a minor loss of transactional atomicity in update_task.

problems.description: rate_limit_key() re-implements JWT decoding inline instead of reusing the existing authenticate_request/verify-token logic, duplicating auth parsing in two places and risking drift between them.

TaskRepository.list_for_owner() return contract changed from a plain list to a (rows, total) tuple; any caller besides app.py would silently break, and the change isn't surfaced in the diff beyond the single call site.

Keyset pagination keys the cursor on id alone while the ORDER BY is created_at DESC, id DESC; if created_at is not strictly monotonic with id (backdated/importer rows), pages can skip or duplicate entries — a composite (created_at, id) cursor would be correct.
Every page runs a separate COUNT(*) over the owner's full task set, which scales with total rows rather than page size; acceptable at this scale but worth noting for large datasets.
Tests override private limiter internals (limiter._storage and limiter._limiter.storage) instead of configuring the limiter via public API; brittle coupling to implementation details.

strengths: User-scoped rate limiting keyed on the JWT subject with IP fallback is a correct, idiomatic cross-cutting security improvement.
Cursor/keyset pagination avoids deep-offset performance cliffs and the limit+1 + has_more pattern is done correctly.
Solid test coverage for both features, including the 429 + Retry-After path and the pagination boundary.
Config is environment-driven (RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_URI) consistent with existing config style; net smell count dropped by 5.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive commit that adds well-tested rate limiting and keyset pagination, though it duplicates existing JWT decode logic, changes the repository return contract, and the convention score of 0.71 largely reflects pre-existing violations in files this diff never touched (celery_config.py, notifications.py) rather than new ones.

compounding_issues: Session 1 greenfield discarded the seed's entire auth layer (260→142 LOC), forcing Session 2 to re-implement authentication from scratch (JWT vs. the seed's token-table design) instead of building on existing code
The nullable owner_id migration (Session 2) permanently orphans any pre-migration legacy tasks with no owner, a tradeoff accepted rather than a data-backfill
Session 4/5 committed __pycache__/*.pyc binaries and a tasks.db database into git (hygiene debt that a .gitignore only addressed later)
No persistence abstraction existed before Session 4, so the repository extraction had to be a carefully behavior-preserving refactor to avoid breaking the auth/ownership logic from Sessions 2-3
key_decisions: JWT (PyJWT HS256) stateless auth plus per-task owner_id with a backward-compatible nullable-column ALTER TABLE migration for pre-existing data
Introducing a BaseRepository ABC with TaskRepository/UserRepository and a custom UsernameAlreadyExistsError (Session 4), keeping all DB access out of the route layer
Celery-based async completion notifications with deliberate graceful degradation (a broker outage must not fail the task update)
Per-user rate limiting keyed on the JWT subject (IP fallback) and cursor-based pagination returning total/next_cursor (Session 5)
Multi-file modularization across sessions (app.py / notifications.py / celery_config.py / repositories.py) instead of one monolithic file
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. Session 1 delivered a bare SQLite task CRUD API with minimal structure; Session 2 added real value with JWT auth, per-owner isolation, and a tested data migration (growing the suite to include migration-preservation tests); Session 3 added Celery integration with careful failure handling; Session 4 was a disciplined behavior-preserving refactor that extracted a clean repository layer while keeping all tests green; Session 5 capped it with production cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, cursor pagination) and matching tests. The final state runs a clean 11-test suite, and each session's feature built directly on the abstractions the previous session established.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, steadily improving multi-session story that progressed greenfield → feature → integration → refactor → cross-cutting, with only minor early waste (re-inventing auth the seed had provided) and git-hygiene debt as compounding costs.
